checks.text: Docked with 7.3 L of gel in the trough and the arm folded, womb and tail float as one egg at z -142 mm, level with 0.2 L in the trim tank, roll GM 191 mm.

Trim stays within 0.07 deg while the gel moves from the tail into the trough and within 0.00 deg after (printing 0.00, baby at the lip -0.00, after the birth 0.00; positive is stern down); the tail pump moves water in the trim tank (0.2 L folded, 4.1 L printing, 6.0 L at the lip, 8 L tank).
The birth opening stays above the water: the lowest point of the opening is 82 mm or more above the waterline in every state.

Docking height: the womb takes 23.2 L of water into two ballast bags beside the trough and floats at z -142 mm like the tail (z -142 mm); the faces meet within the 23 mm the cone captures (womb trim -0.7 deg). The bags let out as much water as gel comes in, so the egg keeps the docking height.
Before docking the bottom of the docking bore is 13 mm above water on the womb and 18 mm on the tail.
Docked, the bottom of the bore sits 17 mm above the waterline, inside the dock seal.

Gel trough (the sketch of 21 Nov): 270 x 180 mm inside, floor at z -285 mm, gel surface at z -135 mm, so the gel covers the folded print by 15 mm and leaves 15 mm under the belly. 7.3 L of gel, against 30.9 L to fill the womb bottom to the same level and 24.1 L at the least; the rest of the womb stays air. The flat floor hangs up to 39 mm under the curved hull, a shallow keel.

Gel supply: carrying the 7.3 L in the tail would sink the tail about 37 mm and put the bore under water before docking, so the tail keeps a 1 L buffer and the gel pump, the buffer is topped up through the dock line from a shore tank, and the gel goes through the bottom channel into the floor of the trough: 2.0 L/min through 0.9 m of 12 mm line needs 29 kPa against the 100 kPa of the pump class (Bingham flow, plastic viscosity 0.3 Pa s, an estimate); the trough fills from below in 3.6 min, level by itself.
The gel surface (z -135 mm) is 10 mm under the bottom of the docking bore.

The kit stays where the arm sets the kit: the kit is lighter than the gel, and 2.5 Pa of yield stress is enough to stop the kit rising (the gel has 25 Pa); the three saddle feet sit in three cups on the seat.

Docking ring, thin: a 4 mm PETG lip flush with the shell on each face, plus three 44 x 44 mm bosses 6 mm thick behind the 40 x 40 x 4 mm steel pads of the FluxGrip FG40 magnets. At the worst dock load of 72 N per magnet (v2 design) a boss bends to 5 MPa, and at the full 250 N rating to 19 MPa, against about 50 MPa for PETG.

Birth opening rim, thin: a 3 mm PETG lip rolled into the 3 mm shell, no magnets. The rim only carries the friction of the body sliding out (under 4 N) and keeps the D 280 opening round; the stern plate already carries the shell loads.

Arm out of the tail: the boom slides the folded DexArm (passage pose, stem turned forward) through the bore; the arm stays inside R 110 mm of the R 125 mm bore, closest 15.2 mm to any part (bore lip).
Reach over the whole print: all 60345 G-code points reached within 0.000 mm inside the official joint ranges (base -17 to 20, J1 6 to 80, J2 76 to 84 deg), boom A from -318 to -10 mm.

Collisions while printing: every link and the tool stay 15.8 mm or more from the shell, the trough walls, the walls, chute and cradle (closest: B Fix to the bore lip; the needle in the work is left out).
Only the stem enters the gel: the lowest link is 40 mm and the tool head 16 mm above the gel surface.
After the kit is set, the stem misses every kit part; closest pass 3.4 mm.
Kit pick and place with the suction module: reached within 0.07 mm, closest 11.4 mm (EE to the womb shell); module and kit, or module and the worst gel load, 320 g, under the 500 g payload.

Suction hold: a 15 mm cup at 35 kPa holds 6.19 N in theory and 3.71 N at a 60 % seal on the flat silicone face of the saddle (46 x 50 mm). Loads on the cup: 1.11 N carrying in air; -0.94 N while lowering through the gel (the gel pushes the kit into the cup: 0.87 N of yield bearing and side shear against 1.05 N of weight less 1.12 N of buoyancy); 0.81 N if the kit had to be lifted back out of the gel. Safety factor 3.3 on the worst case. A sideways move in the gel would load the cup with 0.54 N in shear and peel, so the path only moves the kit sideways in air.
Tool change 1 (needle module to suction module) at the rack on the docking wall, boom at x -220 mm: reached within 0.00 mm, closest 12.9 mm (tool to the rack forks, up, clear of the rack); 55 s.
Tool change 2 (suction module to needle module) at the rack on the docking wall, boom at x -220 mm: reached within 0.00 mm, closest 12.9 mm (tool to the rack forks, up, clear of the rack); 54 s.

Module mount: the Rotrics quick release (press the end effector button, pull the module off; push the next one on until the latch clicks; 5 pin module port). A pin on each fork presses the button as the module settles, so the change needs no extra motor. Rotrics asks for the arm to be off during a change; a powered change through the rack needs a bench test, otherwise the tail switches the arm off for the 1.5 s of the release, with the arm resting on the brakes in that pose (both untested).

Reach and clearance along the push: reached within 15.77 mm, closest 0.2 mm (tool to the womb shell). The septum and push boss sit 20 mm below the axis on the tail cap, so the arm pushes lower and the forearm keeps clear of the shell under the opening.
When the arm lets go, the needle tip is 99 mm from the rim of the opening.

Push while inflating: no segment opens inside the womb. The air is metered by the push position (12 L/min pump), so each of the 8 segments opens only after the segment has passed out through the stern opening, front first; the push waits for the air.
The folded part passes the D 280 opening: the body slides over the lip, where the chute runs flush into the rim, and keeps -49 mm to the rest of the rim (folded diameter 120 mm).

Arm force within the DexArm payload: peak 4.18 N against 4.91 N (500 g). Before the first segment is out the folded body (0.72 kg after the gel is drained) climbs the chute on the arm alone: 4.18 N at friction 0.2; once a segment opens outside, the pressure on the rim pulls the body out (up to 2.3 N) and the arm force falls.

Margin on friction: the chute is lined with PTFE film and wet with gel (friction 0.2 assumed, bench test needed), and the trapped gel is drained first, so the whole folded body (0.72 kg) on the steepest part of the chute (22 deg) needs 3.95 N at friction 0.2 and 4.61 N at 0.3, within the 4.91 N payload; 5.26 N at 0.4 and 6.57 N at 0.6 would not be (bare PETG).

Drain before the climb: air through the needle at 450 Pa pushes the trapped gel out of a 6 mm duckbill vent in the nose: 238 Pa shears the gel plug inside the folded body, 212 Pa drives 0.31 L/min through the vent, 0.67 L out in 2.2 min, 0.12 L left in the fold corners (estimate). The gel round the body keeps the folds shut: opening a fold inside the gel needs about 600 Pa. The body goes from 1.40 to 0.72 kg.
Stem bending at the peak push: 12G needle 127 MPa, 6 x 4 mm tube 34 MPa, against about 200 MPa yield for 304 stainless.

All the air goes in through the arm: a pump in the tail feeds an air line along the boom and the arm to the 12G needle in the valve on the tail cap; 12 L/min needs about 4.8 kPa, well within a 20 kPa diaphragm pump. No other source fills the body.

The needle stays in the valve until the body has all its air: the arm pushes until the tail end reaches x 265 mm, the farthest it reaches with the needle boss 20 mm low and 10 mm to the shell, then holds there from 304 s while the rest of the air goes in (the segments still inside are at the narrow tail end and pass the rim as they open); full at 446 s, then the needle comes out and the arm lets go. While holding, the opened part pulls the needle outward with at most 0.26 N, against a few newtons of grip of a 12G needle in a silicone septum (estimate, bench test).

The sketch path (inflate to full size inside the womb, then leave through the high opening) does not work: the full body is 376 mm across against the 280 mm opening, and in air the 1.40 kg body would have to be lifted 220 mm, while the DexArm payload is 0.5 kg. The birth therefore keeps the push while inflating: folded inside, opening segment by segment outside.

Telescopic boom at full reach: 495 mm beyond the rail end; the second stage is an 80 x 16 mm aluminum box tube with a 2 mm wall (3.4 times stiffer in bending than the old 120 x 6 mm plate, and lighter), tip deflection under the arm and push 0.9 mm; the tube corner passes the bore at radius 113 of 125 mm.
Dock: the tail arrives at 10 mm/s on two small pumps; the cone centers the collar and the three FluxGrip magnets switch on after contact and hold 750 N.

Full size newborn: 0.53 m long and 0.37 m across, 41 L (the womb inside is 0.75 m long, 0.70 wide, 0.58 tall: 70 % of the length, 54 % of the width). Limited by the skin area that packs into the printed 0.20 x 0.12 m envelope and by a stable 25 percent stretch.

The newborn floats upright: 0.72 kg dry would float 28 mm deep, so the kit pumps take 1.4 L of water into a belly pocket; then 50 mm deep with the kit pumps 50 mm under water, centre of gravity 128 mm under the axis.
The newborn swims on the two kit jets at 0.12 m/s.

Small pumps (DFRobot FIT0800, 100 L/h, 4 mm jet, 0.026 N each): the docked egg swims at 0.09 m/s on four and turns at 1.3 deg/s on one; the womb alone swims at 0.06 m/s and turns at 4.2 deg/s. Slow, as accepted.
